Module Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this module, you will be able to:

  1. Synthesize the major theoretical approaches to educational supervision, including scientific management, democratic, and contemporary models (Course Objective 1).
  2. Trace the historical evolution of supervision from inspection-based models to collaborative, growth-oriented frameworks.
  3. Analyze the importance of organizational culture and climate in creating effective learning environments (Course Objective 8).
  4. Distinguish between supervision for evaluation and supervision for professional growth.
  5. Apply foundational supervisory concepts to your current or anticipated leadership practice.
Standards Alignment: This module aligns with PSEL 2015 Standards 2 (Ethics and Professional Norms) and 7 (Professional Community for Teachers and Staff), NELP Standards 7.4, and CT CCL Code 2.A and 3.B.

Section 1: What Is Supervision?

Supervision in education is far more than a set of administrative procedures. At its core, supervision represents the organized efforts of school leaders to support, guide, and enhance the professional practice of teachers and staff in service of improved student learning. Understanding what supervision is—and what it is not—provides the essential foundation for everything we will study in this course.

Defining Supervision

Scholars have defined educational supervision in multiple ways, each reflecting evolving assumptions about teaching, learning, and leadership. Early definitions framed supervision primarily as inspection—a hierarchical process in which authority figures observed and judged teachers' compliance with prescribed methods. Over time, the field shifted toward more collaborative, growth-oriented definitions.

Glickman, Gordon, and Ross-Gordon (2018) define supervision as the actions that enable teachers to improve instruction for students. This definition emphasizes three important ideas: supervision is about action, it is focused on improvement, and its ultimate purpose is student learning. Sergiovanni and Starratt (2007) further expanded the concept by describing supervision as an opportunity to build a community of learners among educators—one in which professional growth is continuous and reciprocal.

Key Distinction: Supervision for evaluation focuses on accountability—determining whether a teacher meets performance standards. Supervision for development focuses on growth—helping teachers expand their professional knowledge, skills, and reflective practices. Effective leaders must navigate both purposes while maintaining trust.

The Dual Purpose of Supervision

One of the enduring tensions in the field is the dual role of the supervisor as both evaluator and supporter. When supervisors are responsible for both summative evaluation (rating performance) and formative development (fostering growth), teachers may hesitate to reveal areas of weakness or uncertainty. Nolan and Hoover (2011) argue that organizations must create structures that clearly differentiate between evaluative and developmental supervision so that teachers feel safe engaging in authentic professional growth.

This tension is not merely theoretical. In your own schools, you may have experienced or witnessed the discomfort that arises when a principal who conducts annual evaluations also claims to be a "coach." Understanding how to manage this duality—through clear communication, separate processes, and a culture of trust—will be a recurring theme throughout this course.

Supervision vs. Related Concepts

It is important to distinguish supervision from related concepts that are sometimes used interchangeably but carry distinct meanings:

Administration refers to the management of organizational structures, policies, and resources. While administrators may also supervise, administration encompasses a broader set of responsibilities including budgeting, scheduling, and compliance.

Evaluation is a subset of supervision focused specifically on making judgments about teacher performance against established criteria. It often results in formal ratings, documentation, and employment decisions.

Instructional leadership is a broader concept that includes supervision but also encompasses curriculum development, assessment practices, resource allocation for instruction, and establishing an academic vision for the school.

Coaching is a specific supervisory approach that emphasizes ongoing, job-embedded, non-evaluative support. Coaching may occur within a supervisory framework but is typically separate from formal evaluation.

Section 2: Historical Evolution of Supervision

To understand where supervision is today, leaders must understand where it has been. The history of educational supervision in the United States reflects broader social, political, and philosophical shifts in how we think about teaching, learning, and authority.

The Inspection Era (1600s–1900)

The earliest forms of supervision in American education were rooted in inspection and compliance. In colonial New England, local committees of clergy and community leaders visited schools to ensure that teachers maintained proper moral character and adhered to the approved curriculum—primarily religious instruction. The supervisor's role was to inspect and judge, not to support or develop.

As public schooling expanded through the 19th century, the inspection model persisted. Superintendents and principals observed classrooms looking for deviations from prescribed teaching methods. Teachers had little professional autonomy, and the relationship between supervisor and teacher was fundamentally hierarchical.

Scientific Management (Early 1900s)

The early 20th century brought Frederick Taylor's principles of scientific management into education. Just as Taylor advocated for standardized procedures in factories, education reformers sought to standardize teaching through prescribed methods, efficiency measures, and close oversight. Supervisors were tasked with ensuring that teachers followed the "one best method" of instruction.

While this era introduced systematic observation to supervision, it treated teaching as a technical act that could be optimized through standardization rather than as a complex professional practice requiring judgment, creativity, and contextual responsiveness.

The Democratic and Human Relations Movement (1930s–1960s)

Beginning in the 1930s, influenced by the work of John Dewey on democratic education and the Hawthorne studies on human relations in organizations, a new vision of supervision emerged. Scholars like Kimball Wiles argued that supervision should be democratic, cooperative, and focused on helping teachers grow. The supervisor's role shifted from inspector to helper and facilitator.

This period established several principles that remain central to contemporary supervision: the importance of treating teachers as professionals, the value of collaboration, and the recognition that effective supervision requires strong interpersonal relationships built on mutual respect.

Clinical Supervision (1960s–1980s)

Morris Cogan and Robert Goldhammer developed the clinical supervision model at Harvard University in the 1960s. Clinical supervision introduced a structured cycle of pre-observation conference, observation, analysis, and post-observation conference. For the first time, supervision had a clearly articulated process designed to promote reflective dialogue between supervisor and teacher.

The clinical model represented a significant advance because it positioned the teacher as an active participant in the supervisory process rather than a passive subject of inspection. However, critics noted that in practice, clinical supervision was often reduced to a bureaucratic checklist rather than the reflective partnership its creators intended.

Contemporary Approaches (1990s–Present)

Contemporary supervision integrates insights from all previous eras while adding new dimensions. Differentiated supervision (Glatthorn, 1997) recognizes that teachers at different career stages and skill levels require different forms of support. Developmental supervision (Glickman et al., 2018) matches supervisory approaches to teachers' developmental levels. Culturally responsive supervision (Jacobs, 2006) emphasizes the need for supervisors to understand how culture, identity, and power dynamics shape the supervisory relationship.

Today's effective supervisors draw from multiple models and adapt their approach based on the needs of individual teachers, the context of the school, and the goals of the educational community.

Section 3: Theoretical Approaches to Supervision

Supervisory practice is grounded in theory. The theoretical lens a leader adopts—consciously or unconsciously—shapes every aspect of how they interact with teachers, what they observe, what they value, and what they believe about professional growth. In this section, we examine the major theoretical frameworks that inform supervision.

Key Theorists and Their Contributions

Carl Glickman — Developmental Supervision

Glickman's developmental model proposes that supervisors should match their approach to a teacher's level of development, commitment, and expertise. He identifies a continuum of supervisory behaviors—from directive (providing clear guidance) to collaborative (working as partners) to nondirective (facilitating the teacher's own problem-solving). The effective supervisor diagnoses where a teacher falls on this continuum and adjusts accordingly.

Morris Cogan & Robert Goldhammer — Clinical Supervision

The clinical supervision cycle remains one of the most widely used frameworks. Its five phases—pre-observation conference, observation, analysis and strategy, supervision conference, and post-conference analysis—create a structured yet flexible process for examining teaching practice and promoting reflective growth.

Thomas Sergiovanni — Moral Leadership

Sergiovanni challenged the field to move beyond bureaucratic and technical approaches to supervision. He argued that schools are fundamentally moral communities and that supervision should be grounded in shared values, professional virtue, and a commitment to the common good. His concept of "moral authority" emphasizes that the most powerful form of leadership comes from shared purpose rather than positional power.

Noreen Garman — Interpretive Supervision

Garman advanced a phenomenological approach to supervision, arguing that understanding teaching requires more than observation checklists. Supervisors must interpret the meaning behind teaching acts, understand the teacher's intentions, and engage in deep dialogue about the lived experience of teaching and learning.

Robert Anderson & Karolyn Snyder — Clinical Supervision Refinement

Anderson and Snyder refined the clinical model by emphasizing that the purpose of the pre-observation conference is to understand the teacher's plans and concerns, that observation should focus on data collection (not judgment), and that the post-conference should be a collaborative analysis of evidence. Their work helped preserve the integrity of clinical supervision against its bureaucratic dilution.

Allan Glatthorn — Differentiated Supervision

Glatthorn argued that a single supervisory model cannot serve all teachers effectively. His differentiated supervision framework provides multiple pathways: clinical supervision for teachers who need intensive support, cooperative professional development for experienced teachers, self-directed development for highly skilled professionals, and administrative monitoring for basic quality assurance.

Connecting Theory to Practice

These theoretical approaches are not mutually exclusive. Effective supervisors develop what Glickman calls a "supervisory platform"—a personal philosophy that integrates insights from multiple theories. Your supervisory platform reflects your beliefs about teaching, learning, teacher development, and the purpose of schooling. Throughout this course, you will develop and refine your own supervisory platform as you encounter each framework in greater depth.

Reflective Prompt: Consider a supervisor you have worked with. Which theoretical approach best describes their practice? Was it effective? What would you have changed?

Section 4: School Culture, Climate, and Effective Supervision

Supervision does not occur in a vacuum. The culture and climate of a school profoundly shape whether supervisory efforts succeed or fail. A school with a toxic culture—characterized by distrust, isolation, and fear—will undermine even the most well-designed supervisory system. Conversely, a healthy culture of trust, collaboration, and continuous improvement amplifies the impact of effective supervision.

Defining Culture and Climate

Organizational culture refers to the deep-seated beliefs, values, norms, and assumptions that govern how people think and behave within a school. Culture is often described as "the way we do things here." It is transmitted through stories, rituals, symbols, and the informal expectations that new members absorb through socialization.

Organizational climate refers to the prevailing attitudes, feelings, and behaviors that characterize a school at any given time. Climate is often more immediately observable than culture—it is the "feel" of a school when you walk through the doors. Climate can change relatively quickly in response to leadership actions, events, or policy changes, while culture evolves more slowly.

The Supervisor's Role in Shaping Culture

School leaders who serve as supervisors play a critical role in creating and sustaining a culture that supports professional growth. Key elements include:

Psychological Safety: Amy Edmondson's (2019) research on psychological safety demonstrates that people in organizations perform best when they feel safe to take risks, make mistakes, and speak honestly without fear of punishment. Supervisors who create psychologically safe environments find that teachers are more willing to try new strategies, request feedback, and engage in honest reflection about their practice.

Trust: Bryk and Schneider's (2002) research on relational trust in schools identified four components: respect, personal regard, competence in core responsibilities, and personal integrity. When these elements are present, teachers are more likely to embrace supervision as a growth opportunity rather than a threat.

Collaborative Norms: DuFour and Fullan (2013) argue that the most effective schools function as professional learning communities where teachers regularly collaborate to examine student work, share practices, and collectively solve instructional problems. Supervision in such schools becomes embedded in the daily fabric of professional life rather than an isolated, periodic event.

Healthy vs. Toxic School Environments

Hoy and Miskel (2013) identify characteristics that distinguish healthy schools from unhealthy ones. Healthy schools exhibit institutional integrity (the school is protected from unreasonable external demands), collegial leadership (the principal is supportive and sets clear expectations), high academic emphasis, and strong teacher affiliation (teachers feel connected to each other and to the school). In contrast, toxic environments are characterized by professional isolation, blame cultures, inconsistent expectations, and the absence of meaningful professional development.

Leadership Implication: Before implementing any supervisory system, effective leaders assess the existing culture and climate. Attempting to implement rigorous supervision in a school lacking trust is likely to generate resistance rather than growth. Building relational trust must come first.

Case Study: Riverside Elementary

Scenario: A New Principal Confronts a Supervision Challenge

Dr. Maria Santos has just been appointed principal of Riverside Elementary, a pre-K through 5 school serving a diverse community of 450 students. The school has experienced significant leadership turnover—Dr. Santos is the fourth principal in six years. Teacher morale is low, and many veteran teachers describe a culture of distrust and professional isolation.

During her first few weeks, Dr. Santos reviews the school's supervisory records. She discovers that the previous principals conducted observations infrequently and inconsistently. Some teachers have not received a formal observation in over two years. When observations did occur, they followed a rigid checklist format with no pre- or post-conference. Several teachers confided that they viewed observations as "gotcha" events rather than opportunities for growth.

Dr. Santos has 28 classroom teachers ranging from first-year novices to 25-year veterans. She is expected to implement the district's new teacher evaluation system, which requires two formal observations per year for all teachers and three for non-tenured teachers. She also wants to build a collaborative professional culture that supports ongoing teacher development.

Guiding Questions for Analysis:

  1. Using what you know about school culture and climate, how would you characterize Riverside Elementary? What specific indicators of a toxic or unhealthy environment are present?
  2. Drawing on Bryk and Schneider's framework of relational trust, what steps should Dr. Santos take in her first 90 days to begin building trust with the teaching staff?
  3. How might Dr. Santos address the tension between her evaluative responsibilities (the district's required observations) and her goal of creating a growth-oriented supervisory culture?
  4. Using Glatthorn's differentiated supervision model, how might Dr. Santos design a supervisory approach that meets the needs of both novice and veteran teachers?
  5. What theoretical framework(s) from this module would you recommend Dr. Santos use as the foundation for her supervisory approach, and why?

Note: You will discuss this case study during our synchronous session. Prepare notes on your analysis to share with your small group.

Key Terms

Clinical Supervision A structured supervisory model involving pre-conference, observation, analysis, post-conference, and reflection phases designed to promote collaborative examination of teaching practice.
Developmental Supervision An approach that matches supervisory behaviors (directive, collaborative, nondirective) to teachers' levels of development, commitment, and expertise.
Differentiated Supervision A framework providing multiple supervisory pathways (clinical, cooperative, self-directed, monitoring) to meet the diverse needs of teachers.
Formative Supervision Supervisory activities focused on supporting teacher growth and improvement, distinct from summative evaluation.
Organizational Culture The deep-seated beliefs, values, norms, and assumptions that govern behavior within a school; "the way we do things here."
Organizational Climate The prevailing attitudes, feelings, and behaviors that characterize a school's environment at a given time; the "feel" of a school.
Psychological Safety A shared belief that the environment is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, enabling honest dialogue and authentic learning.
Relational Trust The social exchanges and interpersonal bonds—built on respect, regard, competence, and integrity—that enable productive collaboration in schools.
Summative Evaluation Formal assessment of teacher performance against established standards, typically resulting in a rating or employment decision.
Supervisory Platform A leader's personal philosophy of supervision that integrates beliefs about teaching, learning, and professional development.
